lesson.title: Escaping the Delimiter: Byte Stuffing in Character-Oriented Protocols
lesson.summary: Byte stuffing solves framing's false delimiter problem for byte oriented protocols by inserting a reserved escape byte before any accidental occurrence of the frame's flag byte, exactly the way PPP protects its 0x7E flag with a 0x7D escape.
lesson.body:
Bit stuffing solves the false delimiter problem for protocols that treat data as a raw stream of individual bits, but many protocols, especially older, character oriented ones, work in terms of whole bytes instead. For these protocols, byte stuffing solves the identical underlying problem, framing needs a reserved marker byte, and real data might coincidentally contain that exact byte, using a byte level trick rather than a bit level one.

The idea is to reserve one byte value as a flag marking the start or end of a frame, and a second reserved byte value as an escape character. If the flag byte, or the escape byte itself, ever appears naturally inside the data being sent, the transmitter precedes it with the escape byte before transmitting it, and typically also modifies it slightly so that even the escape byte followed by real data can never be confused with a deliberate escape sequence. The receiver, upon seeing the escape byte, knows the very next byte is not a delimiter or another escape but real data that needs to be restored to its original value, and it removes the escape byte and reverses the modification.

PPP, the Point to Point Protocol commonly used for byte oriented links, provides a precise real example. PPP uses 0x7E as its flag byte and 0x7D as its control escape byte. If the data stream naturally contains a 0x7E byte, the transmitter replaces it with the two byte sequence 0x7D followed by 0x5E, where 0x5E is simply 0x7E with its sixth bit flipped, an operation written as 0x7E XOR 0x20. If the data contains an actual 0x7D byte, it is replaced the same way, with 0x7D followed by 0x5D. The receiver watches for 0x7D in the incoming stream. Whenever it sees one, it discards that escape byte, takes the byte that follows, flips its sixth bit back with the same XOR 0x20 operation, and treats the result as the original data byte. An older, similar protocol called SLIP used the same basic idea with its own reserved END and escape byte values.

Byte stuffing has a different worst case overhead profile than bit stuffing. Because it operates on whole bytes rather than individual bits, a run of data that happens to consist entirely of the flag byte value expands to exactly double its original size, one escape byte for every original byte, whereas typical binary or text data expands only slightly, since the flag and escape byte values are just two specific values out of 256 possible byte values and rarely dominate real payloads. Byte stuffing also tends to be simpler to implement in software that already processes data one byte at a time, which is part of why older, simpler serial line protocols like PPP and SLIP favored it over bit level manipulation.

Both bit stuffing and byte stuffing exist purely to guarantee that framing delimiters are unambiguous no matter what data happens to be sent, and the choice between them comes down to whether the underlying link is naturally organized around individual bits or whole bytes. Either way, the receiver always undoes the stuffing before handing the frame's actual contents up to higher layers, so the extra bits or bytes are purely a transport level detail invisible to everything above the data link layer.
